questions.objective: 3.6 Apply 2-rescuer adult CPR roles, switching, and feedback
questions.text: During adult CPR practice, how long should a compressor switch take?

answers.text: As long as the rescuers need to rest
At least 30 seconds
Less than 5 seconds
About 1 minute

explanations.a: Rest should be managed without long compression pauses.
explanations.b: A long switch reduces compression fraction.
explanations.c: The manual notes the compressor switch should take less than 5 seconds. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: A 1-minute switch is too long.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.6 Apply 2-rescuer adult CPR roles, switching, and feedback
questions.text: What should the airway rescuer do during 2-rescuer adult CPR?

answers.text: Press on the compressor's hands during compressions
Ignore chest rise while giving breaths
Give continuous forceful breaths during compressions
Open the airway, give breaths, watch chest rise, and avoid excessive ventilation

explanations.a: This can interfere with proper compression technique.
explanations.b: Chest rise helps confirm effective breaths.
explanations.c: Excessive ventilation can cause harm and interrupt CPR.
explanations.d: The airway rescuer supports ventilation while the compressor maintains high-quality compressions. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.1 Identify adult chest compression hand placement and body position
questions.text: A rescuer prepares for adult CPR. Where on the chest should the heel of the dominant hand be placed?

answers.text: On the lower half of the sternum (breastbone) at the center of the chest
On the upper third of the sternum near the manubrium
On the right side of the chest over the lung fields
Below the xiphoid process on the upper abdomen

explanations.a: AHA Part 2: heel of the hand on the lower half of the sternum, in the center of the chest.
explanations.b: Upper-third placement is too high and reduces compression effectiveness.
explanations.c: Right-side placement compresses the lung but not the heart effectively.
explanations.d: Compressing on the xiphoid risks fracture and visceral injury.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.1 Identify adult chest compression hand placement and body position
questions.text: A rescuer prepares for adult CPR but cannot place both hands due to limited space. According to AHA Part 2, what alternative may be used?

answers.text: Use a single finger on the sternum
Use the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum — single-hand compression is acceptable when 2-hand placement is not possible
Switch to back blows in this case
Wait until repositioning allows 2-hand placement, even if it takes minutes

explanations.a: One finger cannot generate the force required for adult compressions.
explanations.b: AHA recognizes that single-hand compression is appropriate when constrained, although 2-hand stacked is the default.
explanations.c: Back blows are FBAO maneuvers, not arrest care.
explanations.d: Multi-minute delay in compressions is unacceptable; adapt position.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.2 Apply adult compression rate, depth, recoil, and compression fraction targets
questions.text: According to AHA Part 2, what is the target adult compression RATE?

answers.text: 60–80 per minute
100–120 compressions per minute
140–160 per minute
200 per minute, as fast as possible

explanations.a: 60–80 is below the target and reduces cardiac output.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: target is 100–120 compressions per minute for adults (and pediatrics).
explanations.c: Above 120 reduces diastolic filling and stroke volume.
explanations.d: 200/min is uncoordinated and reduces depth.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.2 Apply adult compression rate, depth, recoil, and compression fraction targets
questions.text: AHA Part 2 emphasizes "compression fraction." What does this term mean and what target does AHA recommend?

answers.text: The ratio of compressions to breaths in a CPR cycle
The depth of each compression in fractions of an inch
The percentage of total CPR time during which compressions are actively being delivered; AHA recommends a compression fraction of >60–80% to minimize interruptions
The fraction of rescuers participating in compressions

explanations.a: Compression-to-breath ratio is a separate variable (30:2 single rescuer).
explanations.b: Compression depth is reported in inches/cm, not as "compression fraction."
explanations.c: AHA Part 2: compression fraction = % of CPR time with active compressions; >60% is the minimum standard, with >80% as a high-quality target. Minimizing interruption pauses is critical.
explanations.d: Compression fraction is a time metric, not a personnel metric.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.2 Apply adult compression rate, depth, recoil, and compression fraction targets
questions.keyword: full chest recoil venous return preload
questions.text: During adult CPR, why does AHA emphasize allowing FULL chest recoil between compressions?

answers.text: Full recoil is decorative and does not affect outcome

Full recoil allows the chest to spring back, reducing intrathoracic pressure and creating the negative pressure that draws blood back into the heart for the next compression — leaning on the chest impairs venous return
Full recoil cools the chest down between compressions
Full recoil is only relevant in pediatric CPR

explanations.a: Full recoil has measurable physiologic effect, not cosmetic.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: full chest recoil is necessary to allow venous return — leaning during recoil increases intrathoracic pressure and reduces preload, lowering cardiac output during the next compression.
explanations.c: Compressions do not affect chest temperature in any clinically meaningful way.
explanations.d: Full recoil is critical in adult, pediatric, and infant CPR.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.3 Identify adult compression-to-breath ratio and interruption limits
questions.text: According to AHA Part 2, what is the compression-to-breath ratio for SINGLE-rescuer adult CPR?

answers.text: 30:2 — 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths
15:2 — 15 compressions followed by 2 breaths
5:1 — 5 compressions to 1 breath
50:2 — 50 compressions to 2 breaths

explanations.a: AHA Part 2: 30:2 is the universal adult ratio (single or 2 rescuer).
explanations.b: 15:2 is the pediatric 2-rescuer ratio, not adult.
explanations.c: 5:1 is not used in modern AHA guidelines.
explanations.d: 50:2 is not an AHA ratio.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.3 Identify adult compression-to-breath ratio and interruption limits
questions.text: According to AHA Part 2, what is the maximum acceptable INTERRUPTION in compressions for any reason during adult CPR?

answers.text: 30 seconds
Less than 10 seconds — interruptions for rhythm check, AED analysis, pulse check, etc., should each be ≤10 seconds
60 seconds during AED analysis
No limit; interrupt as needed

explanations.a: 30 seconds is too long; AHA targets ≤10.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: interruptions should each be ≤10 seconds whenever possible — pulse check, rhythm check, AED-analysis transitions all aim for this limit.
explanations.c: 60 seconds far exceeds the AHA target.
explanations.d: AHA explicitly limits interruptions to preserve coronary perfusion pressure.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.3 Identify adult compression-to-breath ratio and interruption limits
questions.text: Per AHA Part 2 BLS guidance, what is the compression-to-breath ratio for 2-RESCUER adult CPR?

answers.text: 15:2 like pediatric 2-rescuer CPR
30:2 — the same as single-rescuer adult CPR

explanations.a: 15:2 applies to pediatric 2-rescuer CPR, not adult.
explanations.b: 50:2 is not an AHA ratio.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2: adult 30:2 ratio applies in both single- and 2-rescuer configurations.
explanations.d: 5:1 is not an AHA ratio.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.4 Open the airway and provide effective adult breaths
questions.text: According to AHA Part 2, how should the rescuer open an unresponsive adult's airway when no neck injury is suspected?

answers.text: Head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver — tilt the forehead back with one hand and lift the chin with two fingers of the other hand
Squeeze the nose and lift the head straight up
Press downward on the throat to expand the airway
Bend the head fully forward with the chin on the chest

explanations.a: AHA Part 2: head-tilt/chin-lift is the standard airway-opening maneuver for non-trauma patients.
explanations.b: Squeezing the nose and lifting the head straight up does not open the airway.
explanations.c: Pressing on the throat compresses, rather than opens, the airway.
explanations.d: Forward chin-on-chest position closes the airway.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.4 Open the airway and provide effective adult breaths
questions.keyword: jaw thrust cervical spine injury airway
questions.text: According to AHA Part 2, what is the appropriate airway maneuver for a suspected cervical-spine injury patient?

answers.text: Head-tilt/chin-lift — same as for non-trauma patients
Jaw thrust — lift the angles of the lower jaw upward and forward without tilting the head, to maintain neutral spine alignment
Hyperextend the neck to maximally open the airway
Manual cervical traction with downward pull

explanations.a: Head-tilt/chin-lift extends the neck and may worsen cervical injury.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: jaw thrust opens the airway without manipulating the cervical spine — preferred when trauma is suspected.
explanations.c: Hyperextension would worsen any cervical injury.
explanations.d: Cervical traction is not part of airway management in lay or initial BLS care.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.4 Open the airway and provide effective adult breaths
questions.keyword: no chest rise reposition airway adult
questions.text: During adult CPR, the rescuer delivers 2 breaths but neither produces visible chest rise. According to AHA Part 2, what is the action?

answers.text: Continue compressions and skip breaths permanently
Reposition the airway (re-perform head-tilt/chin-lift), then attempt 2 more breaths; if still no chest rise, return to compressions and look for a foreign body when next opening the airway
Force 4 more breaths in rapid succession
Inflate the breaths through the nose only

explanations.a: Skipping breaths defeats the purpose of CPR for non-cardiac arrest.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: poor chest rise typically indicates suboptimal airway position; reposition and re-attempt; if still ineffective, suspect FBAO and look in mouth on next breath.
explanations.c: Forcing more breaths without addressing the cause does not help.
explanations.d: Mouth-to-nose ventilation is an alternative when mouth-to-mouth is impractical, not the response to no chest rise.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.4 Open the airway and provide effective adult breaths
questions.text: During mouth-to-mouth ventilation of an adult, the rescuer is unable to maintain a tight seal. According to AHA Part 2, what is the appropriate alternative?

answers.text: Use bare-handed nose pinching only
Skip ventilations until a barrier device is found
Attempt mouth-to-mouth with poor seal regardless

Mouth-to-nose ventilation — close the mouth, seal the rescuer's lips around the patient's nose, and deliver breaths; this is acceptable when mouth-to-mouth is impractical due to seal issues, oral injury, or rescuer comfort

explanations.a: Bare-handed nose pinching alone does not deliver air.
explanations.b: Skipping ventilations indefinitely worsens hypoxic arrest in non-cardiac etiologies.
explanations.c: A poor seal wastes breath volume; an alternative technique is preferred.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2: mouth-to-nose ventilation is an accepted alternative when mouth-to-mouth is impractical (oral injury, seal issues, etc.).

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.5 Use pocket mask and bag-mask ventilation correctly during adult CPR
questions.text: A rescuer uses a pocket mask with one-way valve during adult CPR. According to AHA Part 2, what is the correct technique?

answers.text: Hold the mask loosely against the face

Apply the mask with both hands using the E-C clamp grip — thumb and index finger forming a "C" on the mask, third/fourth/fifth fingers under the jaw forming an "E" — ensuring a tight seal, then deliver breaths through the valve
Hold the mask with one finger on top
Use the mask without aligning it on the face

explanations.a: Loose seal allows air leak and ineffective ventilation.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: E-C clamp technique provides a tight seal and aligns the airway; both hands are used when 2 rescuers are present, or 1 hand when single-rescuer with pocket mask.
explanations.c: Single-finger top hold cannot maintain seal under positive pressure.
explanations.d: Misaligned masks leak; alignment is essential.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.5 Use pocket mask and bag-mask ventilation correctly during adult CPR
questions.text: During 2-rescuer adult CPR using a bag-mask device, who should typically perform the bag-mask ventilation?

answers.text: Whoever is closer to the AED
A dedicated rescuer at the head of the patient, freeing the compressor to focus only on chest compressions
The rescuer with the most strength
No one; bag-mask is single-rescuer technique only

explanations.a: AED proximity does not determine ventilation roles.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: in 2-rescuer CPR, one rescuer compresses, the other manages airway and bag-mask ventilation at the head of the patient; roles allow each rescuer to focus.
explanations.c: Strength is not a role criterion; technique and positioning matter.
explanations.d: Bag-mask works in single- or 2-rescuer settings; 2-rescuer with one at the head is preferred.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.5 Use pocket mask and bag-mask ventilation correctly during adult CPR
questions.text: During bag-mask ventilation in adult CPR, the rescuer notices excessive volume escaping around the mask. According to AHA Part 2, what should be done?

answers.text: Squeeze the bag harder to overcome the leak
Reposition the mask to obtain a tight seal — adjust the E-C clamp grip, ensure the mask is sized correctly, and consider 2-handed mask technique while a second rescuer squeezes the bag
Continue with the leak; some leak is acceptable
Switch to mouth-to-mouth without the mask

explanations.a: Squeezing harder does not address the leak; it just wastes more volume and increases gastric inflation.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: leaks are addressed by improving seal — repositioning, correct sizing, or the 2-rescuer 2-handed mask technique with a separate person squeezing the bag.
explanations.c: Significant leak fails to deliver effective ventilation; do not accept it.
explanations.d: Discarding the mask abandons a useful barrier; fix the seal first.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.6 Apply 2-rescuer adult CPR roles, switching, and feedback
questions.text: During 2-rescuer adult CPR, the team plans for compressor rotation. According to AHA Part 2, when and why should rotation occur?

answers.text: Rotate compressors approximately every 2 minutes (about 5 cycles of 30:2) — fatigue significantly reduces compression depth even when the rescuer does not feel tired
Only rotate when the compressor explicitly says they are tired
Rotate every 30 seconds to keep both rescuers active
Never rotate; consistency matters more than fatigue

explanations.a: AHA Part 2: rotate every 2 minutes (5 cycles 30:2) during the rhythm-check pause; objective compression quality declines within 1–2 minutes even before subjective fatigue is noticed.
explanations.b: Subjective fatigue lags behind objective compression decline; relying on it leads to lower-quality CPR.
explanations.c: Every-30-second rotation interrupts CPR too frequently and reduces compression fraction.
explanations.d: Without rotation, compression quality declines, hurting the patient.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.6 Apply 2-rescuer adult CPR roles, switching, and feedback
questions.keyword: CPR feedback rate depth recoil fraction
questions.text: During 2-rescuer adult CPR, the team uses CPR feedback devices. According to AHA Part 2, what feedback metrics matter most?

answers.text: Loudness of the rescuer's breathing
Compression rate (target 100–120/min), depth (target 2–2.4 in), full recoil (no leaning), and compression fraction (>60–80%) — devices that report these in real time can improve CPR quality
Number of bystanders present
Distance to the AED

explanations.a: Rescuer breathing volume is not a feedback metric.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2: real-time CPR feedback should target rate, depth, recoil, and compression fraction — these correlate with outcome.
explanations.c: Bystander count is not feedback for the active rescuer.
explanations.d: AED distance does not affect CPR quality once compressions are underway.

questions.name: Adult CPR
questions.objective: 3.6 Apply 2-rescuer adult CPR roles, switching, and feedback
questions.keyword: advanced airway adult continuous compressions 1 breath 6 seconds
questions.text: During 2-rescuer adult CPR with an advanced airway in place, how does the AHA recommend ventilations and compressions be coordinated (Part 2/4 update)?

answers.text: Pause compressions every breath, exactly like the 30:2 ratio
Provide ventilations only every 30 compressions
Stop ventilations until ROSC
Continuous compressions at 100–120/min, asynchronous with ventilations at 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) for adults — compressions do NOT pause for breaths once an advanced airway is in place

explanations.a: Pausing compressions for breaths defeats the purpose of placing an advanced airway.
explanations.b: Synchronized 30:2 stops applying once an advanced airway is in place.
explanations.c: Ventilation remains essential during arrest; do not stop until ROSC and adequate spontaneous breathing return.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2/4: with an advanced airway, compressions are continuous; adult ventilation rate is 1 every 6 seconds (10/min) — for pediatric patients, 1 every 2–3 seconds (20–30/min) per the 2020 update.
